## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Uppādanirodhavāra* (Ya 9.2.3) is a constituent section of the *Yamaka*, the sixth book of the Theravāda Abhidhamma Piṭaka [SuttaCentral]. In the systematic architecture of the *Yamaka*, the Process division (*pavattivāra*) analyzes doctrinal categories across three complementary modes: origination (*uppādavāra*), cessation (*nirodhavāra*), and combined origination-and-cessation (*uppādanirodhavāra*) [Gal 2003; Ronkin 2005]. Modern scholars note that this analysis embodies early Buddhist process metaphysics—treating experiential phenomena as dynamic processes rather than enduring substances—and marks what is likely the earliest textual occurrence of the term *khaṇa* denoting the temporal subdivision of a moment into phases of origination (*uppādakkhaṇa*) and dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*) [Gal 2003; Ronkin 2005]. SuttaCentral records one translation in one language for this section [SuttaCentral].
No historical external parallels are cataloged on SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral]. Computationally, DharmaNexus identifies 13,398 formulaic text-reuse matches with 44 other Pali texts [DharmaNexus]. Due to the highly iterative catechismal structure of the *Yamaka*, the closest internal reuse occurs with the adjacent sections of the same chapter, specifically the *Uppādavāra* (Ya 9.2.1, with 3,912 matches) and the *Nirodhavāra* (Ya 9.2.2, with 3,884 matches), as well as corresponding *pavattivāra* sections in other chapters (notably Ya 10.2.1, Ya 5.2.2, Ya 6.2.3, and Ya 3.2.3) and the *Abhidhammamātikāpāḷi* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also generates low-to-moderate cross-language alignments with passages in the Sanskrit *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Chapter 1), its Tibetan translations and sub-commentaries (*Tattvārthā* D4421, *Lakṣaṇānusāriṇī* D4093), the Tibetan *Karmaśataka* (D0340-2), and the Chinese *Ānoufeng jing* (T 58), reflecting shared Abhidharmic discussions of arising and passing away rather than shared textual ancestry [DharmaNexus].
